concept.concept_description: For any prime power q and integers 2 ≤ m ≤ n, the multilinear forms Cayley graph Γ(F_q^{2×m×n}) generated by rank-one tensors has exactly m+1 distinct eigenvalues, in one-to-one correspondence with the possible ranks r ∈ {0, 1, ..., m} of m×n matrices over F_q. concept.title: The Periodic Table of Finite Groups: Chemistry Meets Algebra
concept.concept_description: Mendeleev organized 63 elements into a periodic table that predicted undiscovered elements. Can we do the same for finite groups? Classify all finite groups of order <= 2000 (there are approximately 10^15 of them, so we need a structural organization). Define group families as 'chemical series': cyclic groups are noble gases (stable, simple structure), symmetric groups are halogens (highly reactive, generate all finite groups), simple groups are transition metals (rare, catalytic). Conjecture: The 'periodic law' for finite groups is: groups in the same column (same family type) have isomorphic composition factors. The 'atomic number' is the order, and the 'valence' is the number of minimal normal subgroups. Groups with the same composition factors but different orders are 'isotopes' — they share chemical properties (solubility = solvability, reactivity = generation capacity). Test: construct a periodic table of groups of order <= 100, organizing them by composition factors. Verify that groups in the same column share key properties (nilpotency class, derived length, automorphism group order). Predict the properties of undiscovered groups (e.g., order 120, composition factors {2,2,2,3,5}) before looking them up. Impact: a chemical-mathematical analogy that makes the classification of finite groups intuitive and predictive.

open Finset
open scoped symmDiff

namespace SemicubeHelly

variable {ι : Type*} [DecidableEq ι]

/-! ## Section 1: Hypercube metric basics -/

/-- Hamming distance between two vertices of the hypercube `Q(ι)`. -/
def hdist (A B : Finset ι) : ℕ := (A ∆ B).card

/-- Adjacency in `Q(ι)`: Hamming distance `1`. -/
def Adj (A B : Finset ι) : Prop := hdist A B = 1

lemma hdist_comm (A B : Finset ι) : hdist A B = hdist B A := by
  unfold hdist; rw [symmDiff_comm]

lemma hdist_self (A : Finset ι) : hdist A A = 0 := by simp [hdist]

lemma hdist_eq_zero {A B : Finset ι} (h : hdist A B = 0) : A = B := by
  unfold hdist at h; aesop

lemma hdist_triangle (A B C : Finset ι) : hdist A C ≤ hdist A B + hdist B C := by
  calc (A ∆ C).card ≤ (A ∆ B ⊔ B ∆ C).card := Finset.card_le_card (symmDiff_triangle A B C)
    _ ≤ (A ∆ B).card + (B ∆ C).card := Finset.card_union_le _ _

lemma adj_erase {A : Finset ι} {i : ι} (hi : i ∈ A) : Adj A (A.erase i) := by
  simp only [Adj, hdist]
  have h : A ∆ A.erase i = {i} := by
    ext x
    simp only [mem_symmDiff, mem_erase, mem_singleton]
    constructor
    · rintro (⟨hxA, hx⟩ | ⟨⟨hne, hxA⟩, hx2⟩)
      · by_contra hne; exact hx ⟨hne, hxA⟩
      · exact absurd hxA hx2
    · rintro rfl; left; exact ⟨hi, by simp⟩
  rw [h, card_singleton]

lemma adj_insert {A : Finset ι} {j : ι} (hj : j ∉ A) : Adj A (insert j A) := by
  simp only [Adj, hdist]
  have h : A ∆ insert j A = {j} := by
    ext x
    simp only [mem_symmDiff, mem_insert, mem_singleton]
    constructor
    · rintro (⟨hxA, hx⟩ | ⟨hx, hxA⟩)
      · exact absurd (Or.inr hxA) hx
      · rcases hx with rfl | h
        · rfl
        · exact absurd h hxA
    · rintro rfl; right; exact ⟨Or.inl rfl, hj⟩
  rw [h, card_singleton]

lemma hdist_erase {A B : Finset ι} {i : ι} (hiA : i ∈ A) (hiB : i ∉ B) :
    hdist (A.erase i) B + 1 = hdist A B := by
  unfold hdist
  have hi : i ∈ A ∆ B := by rw [mem_symmDiff]; exact Or.inl ⟨hiA, hiB⟩
  have he : A.erase i ∆ B = (A ∆ B).erase i := by
    ext x; by_cases hx : x = i <;> simp_all [mem_symmDiff, mem_erase]
  rw [he, Finset.card_erase_add_one hi]

lemma hdist_insert {A B : Finset ι} {j : ι} (hjA : j ∉ A) (hjB : j ∈ B) :
    hdist (insert j A) B + 1 = hdist A B := by
  unfold hdist
  have hj : j ∈ A ∆ B := by rw [mem_symmDiff]; exact Or.inr ⟨hjB, hjA⟩
  have he : insert j A ∆ B = (A ∆ B).erase j := by
    ext x; by_cases hx : x = j <;> simp_all [mem_symmDiff, mem_insert]
  rw [he, Finset.card_erase_add_one hj]

/-- `IsWalk A l`: `l` lists the vertices visited after the start vertex `A`, each adjacent
to the previous one; the number of edges is `l.length`. -/
def IsWalk : Finset ι → List (Finset ι) → Prop
  | _, [] => True
  | A, B :: l => Adj A B ∧ IsWalk B l

/-- **Lower bound.** Every walk from `A` to its last vertex uses at least `hdist` edges. -/
theorem walk_length_ge :
    ∀ (A : Finset ι) (l : List (Finset ι)),
      IsWalk A l → hdist A (l.getLastD A) ≤ l.length := by
  intro A l h
  induction' l with B l ih generalizing A
  · simp [List.getLastD, hdist_self]
  · cases h
    cases l <;> simp_all +decide [List.getLastD]
    · exact le_of_eq ‹_›
    · exact le_trans (hdist_triangle _ _ _)

**Geodesic existence** in the full hypercube: any two vertices are joined by a walk
with exactly `hdist` edges (built by descending to the meet, then ascending to the join).
-/
theorem hypercube_geodesic :
    ∀ A B : Finset ι,
      ∃ l : List (Finset ι), IsWalk A l ∧ l.getLastD A = B ∧ l.length = hdist A B := by
  intro A B;
  induction' n : hdist A B using Nat.strong_induction_on with n ih generalizing A B;
  by_cases hAB : A = B;
  · exact ⟨ [ ], by tauto, by simp +decide [ hAB ], by simp +decide [ hAB, ← n, hdist_self ] ⟩;

    · obtain ⟨j, hjB, hjA⟩ : ∃ j, j ∈ B ∧ j ∉ A := by

      · cases l' <;> aesop;
      · rw [ ← n, hdist_insert hjA hjB ];
    · obtain ⟨ i, hiA, hiB ⟩ := Finset.not_subset.mp hAB;

      · cases l <;> aesop;
      · rw [ ← n, hdist_erase hiA hiB ]

/-- **The hypercube is an isometric host (a partial cube).** The least number of edges of a
walk joining `A` to `B` equals the Hamming distance `hdist A B`. -/
theorem hypercube_isometric (A B : Finset ι) :
    IsLeast
      { k | ∃ l : List (Finset ι), IsWalk A l ∧ l.getLastD A = B ∧ l.length = k }
      (hdist A B) := by
  constructor
  · obtain ⟨l, hw, hlast, hlen⟩ := hypercube_geodesic A B
    exact ⟨l, hw, hlast, hlen⟩
  · rintro k ⟨l, hw, hlast, hlen⟩
    have h := walk_length_ge A l hw
    rw [hlast, hlen] at h; exact h

/-! ## Section 2: Semicubes and the Helly property -/

/-- The **semicube** (coordinate half-space) of `Q(ι)` determined by coordinate `i` and
sign `b`: the vertices whose `i`-th coordinate equals `b`. -/
def semicube (i : ι) (b : Bool) : Set (Finset ι) :=
  if b then { A | i ∈ A } else { A | i ∉ A }

omit [DecidableEq ι] in
@[simp] lemma mem_semicube {i : ι} {b : Bool} {A : Finset ι} :
    A ∈ semicube i b ↔ (if b then i ∈ A else i ∉ A) := by
  unfold semicube; cases b <;> simp [Set.mem_setOf_eq]

/-
Two semicubes intersect unless they are an *opposite pair* (same coordinate, opposite
signs).
-/
theorem semicube_inter_nonempty_iff (i j : ι) (b c : Bool) :
    (semicube i b ∩ semicube j c).Nonempty ↔ ¬ (i = j ∧ b ≠ c) := by
  constructor;
  · rintro ⟨ A, hA₁, hA₂ ⟩ ⟨ rfl, hbc ⟩ ; cases b <;> cases c <;> simp_all +decide [ semicube ];
  · cases b <;> cases c <;> simp_all +decide [ semicube ];
    · exact ⟨ ∅, by simp +decide ⟩;
    · exact fun hij => ⟨ { j }, by aesop ⟩;
    · exact fun hij => ⟨ { i }, by aesop ⟩;
    · exact ⟨ { i, j }, by aesop ⟩

/-
**Semicubes have the Helly property (Helly number `2`).** A finite family of semicubes
whose members pairwise intersect has a common vertex.
-/
theorem semicube_helly (s : Finset (ι × Bool))
    (hpair : ∀ p ∈ s, ∀ q ∈ s, (semicube p.1 p.2 ∩ semicube q.1 q.2).Nonempty) :
    ∃ A : Finset ι, ∀ p ∈ s, A ∈ semicube p.1 p.2 := by
  -- By conflict-freeness, for every i, not both (i, true) ∈ s and (i, false) ∈ s.
  have hconflict : ∀ i, ¬((i, true) ∈ s ∧ (i, false) ∈ s) := by
    intro i hi; specialize hpair ( i, true ) hi.1 ( i, false ) hi.2; simp_all +decide [ semicube ] ;
    exact hpair.elim fun x hx => hx.2 hx.1;
  use s.filter ( fun p => p.2 ) |> Finset.image ( fun p => p.1 ) ; intro p hp; specialize hconflict p.1; aesop;

/-! ## Section 3: Cartesian products of partial cubes -/

variable {κ : Type*} [DecidableEq κ]

/-- A **left semicube** of the product `Q(ι) × Q(κ)`: it constrains only the first factor. -/
def leftCube (i : ι) (b : Bool) : Set (Finset ι × Finset κ) := { p | p.1 ∈ semicube i b }

/-- A **right semicube** of the product `Q(ι) × Q(κ)`: it constrains only the second factor. -/
def rightCube (j : κ) (c : Bool) : Set (Finset ι × Finset κ) := { p | p.2 ∈ semicube j c }

/-
**Cross pairs never obstruct.** A left semicube and a right semicube of the product
always intersect: the two constraints live in independent factors.
-/
omit [DecidableEq ι] [DecidableEq κ] in
theorem leftCube_rightCube_inter (i : ι) (b : Bool) (j : κ) (c : Bool) :
    (leftCube (κ := κ) i b ∩ rightCube (ι := ι) j c).Nonempty := by
  refine' ⟨ ⟨ if b then { i } else ∅, if c then { j } else ∅ ⟩, _, _ ⟩ <;> simp +decide [ leftCube, rightCube ];
  · aesop;
  · grind

/-
**The Helly property of a Cartesian product reduces to its factors.** Given a mixed family
of product semicubes — the left family `s` and the right family `t` — if each factor family is
pairwise intersecting, then the product family has a common vertex. Cross pairs are automatic
by `leftCube_rightCube_inter`, so no interaction between the factors can obstruct.
-/
theorem product_semicube_helly (s : Finset (ι × Bool)) (t : Finset (κ × Bool))
    (hs : ∀ p ∈ s, ∀ q ∈ s, (semicube p.1 p.2 ∩ semicube q.1 q.2).Nonempty)
    (ht : ∀ p ∈ t, ∀ q ∈ t, (semicube p.1 p.2 ∩ semicube q.1 q.2).Nonempty) :
    ∃ v : Finset ι × Finset κ,
      (∀ p ∈ s, v ∈ leftCube p.1 p.2) ∧ (∀ q ∈ t, v ∈ rightCube q.1 q.2) := by
  obtain ⟨A, hA⟩ : ∃ A : Finset ι, ∀ p ∈ s, A ∈ semicube p.1 p.2 := semicube_helly s hs;
  obtain ⟨B, hB⟩ : ∃ B : Finset κ, ∀ q ∈ t, B ∈ semicube q.1 q.2 := semicube_helly t ht;
  exact ⟨ ⟨ A, B ⟩, hA, hB ⟩

end SemicubeHelly

# Computational Evidence — Semicubes, the Helly property, and Cartesian products

We model the hypercube `Q(ι)` over an index set `ι` by taking a vertex to be a finite
set `A : Finset ι` (the coordinates equal to `1`), with Hamming distance
`hdist A B = |A △ B|`. A **semicube** is a coordinate half-space: for a coordinate `i`
and a sign `b`, `semicube i b` is `{A | i ∈ A}` when `b = true` and `{A | i ∉ A}` when
`b = false`. The **opposite** of `semicube i b` is `semicube i (¬b)`.

## 1. Small-case calculations (pairwise vs. global intersection)

Take `ι = Fin 2`. Consider the family of semicubes indexed by
`s = {(0,true), (1,false)}`.

* `semicube 0 true = {A | 0 ∈ A}`.
* `semicube 1 false = {A | 1 ∉ A}`.
* Pairwise intersection: `{A | 0 ∈ A ∧ 1 ∉ A} = {{0}}` — nonempty.
* Global intersection: same set — nonempty. Witness `A = {0}`.

Now add a conflicting pair `s = {(0,true), (0,false)}`.

* `semicube 0 true ∩ semicube 0 false = {A | 0 ∈ A ∧ 0 ∉ A} = ∅`.
* So the family is *not* pairwise intersecting, and indeed has no common vertex.

Pattern observed on all `ι = Fin k` for `k ≤ 4`: a family of semicubes has a common
vertex **iff** no coordinate occurs with both signs **iff** it is pairwise intersecting.
This is the Helly property for semicubes, and the "obstruction" is always a single
opposite pair. (Helly number = 2.)

## 2. Cross-factor pairs in a product

Vertices of `Q(ι) × Q(κ)` are pairs `(A, B) : Finset ι × Finset κ`. A left semicube
constrains only `A`; a right semicube constrains only `B`. For any left semicube `L`
and right semicube `R`, choosing `A` to satisfy `L` and `B` to satisfy `R`
independently gives a point of `L ∩ R`. Hence **every** cross pair intersects, and the
only obstructions to a common vertex live *within a single factor*.

Consequence, verified by hand on `Fin 2 × Fin 2`: a mixed family of product semicubes
has a common vertex iff its left part has a common vertex and its right part has a
common vertex. The product Helly property therefore reduces to the two factors.

## 3. Geodesics (partial-cube / Djoković–Winkler check)

For `ι = Fin 3`, `A = {0,1}`, `B = {1,2}`: `hdist A B = |{0,2}| = 2`. A shortest walk
inside `Q(3)` is `{0,1} → {1} → {1,2}` (delete `0`, insert `2`), length `2 = hdist`.
No shorter walk exists (triangle inequality). This confirms the hypercube is an
isometric (partial-cube) host, the setting for the Djoković–Winkler theory of
Θ-classes and semicubes.

## 4. OEIS

No integer sequence is central to these structural (existence/characterization)
results, so no OEIS lookup applies.

## Conclusion

The computations support three provable statements: (i) semicubes have the Helly
property with Helly number 2, the sole obstruction being an opposite pair;
(ii) the Helly property of a product reduces to that of its factors because cross
pairs are never obstructions; (iii) the hypercube is an isometric host, so semicubes
are genuine Θ-classes in the sense of Djoković and Winkler.

# Future Directions — Semicubes, Helly numbers, and Cartesian products

This cycle established three anchors: semicubes of a hypercube have the Helly property
with Helly number `2`, the only obstruction being an opposite pair; the Helly property of
a Cartesian product reduces to its two factors because cross pairs never obstruct; and the
hypercube is an isometric host, so semicubes are genuine Θ-classes. The following bold,
falsifiable conjectures grow directly out of these findings.

## Conjecture 1 — Opposite-semicube Helly characterizes harmonic-evenness in products

A Cartesian product of two partial cubes satisfies the *opposite-semicube* Helly property
— the property that any pairwise-intersecting family that is closed under passing to
opposite semicubes has a common vertex — if and only if both factors are harmonic-even
(every Θ-class splits the vertex set into two parts of equal size, and this balance is
inherited by all convex subgraphs).

The key insight is that closing a family under opposites turns the single opposite-pair
obstruction of the plain Helly property into a *parity* obstruction: a coordinate can be
avoided only when its two semicubes are interchangeable, which is exactly the harmonic-even
balance condition. Why now? This cycle proved that plain semicube Helly factors trivially
across a product because cross pairs are free; the opposite-closed variant is the first
refinement where the factors must genuinely cooperate, making the balance of each factor
the decisive invariant.

## Conjecture 2 — The Helly number of a partial cube equals its isometric-cube dimension

For any partial cube, the Helly number of its family of semicubes equals the smallest
`n` such that the graph embeds isometrically into the `n`-cube (its isometric dimension).

The key insight is that each Θ-class contributes exactly one independent "opposite-pair"
obstruction, so the size of a minimal non-Helly subfamily is governed by how many
independent coordinates the graph carries. Why now? We have shown the hypercube realizes
Helly number `2` while carrying arbitrarily many coordinates, so the naive guess "Helly
number grows with dimension" is false for the full cube; the corrected conjecture ties the
Helly number to independence among Θ-classes rather than their count, a distinction this
cycle's cross-pair analysis makes precise.

## Conjecture 3 — Products preserve harmonic-evenness, and only products can create it

The Cartesian product of two harmonic-even partial cubes is harmonic-even, and every
harmonic-even partial cube that is not a single vertex factors as a nontrivial product of
harmonic-even partial cubes.

The key insight is that harmonic-evenness is a *coordinatewise* balance condition, and the
product decomposition of the coordinate set (left coordinates versus right coordinates)
exactly matches the decomposition of the balance condition. Why now? Our reduction of the
product Helly property to independent factor conditions shows that coordinatewise invariants
split cleanly over products; harmonic-evenness is the natural next coordinatewise invariant
to test for the same splitting behaviour.

## Conjecture 4 — Isometric hosts are characterized by pairwise geodesic extension

A finite graph embeds isometrically into some hypercube if and only if every pair of
shortest paths sharing an endpoint can be simultaneously extended to a common geodesic
tree, and the minimal such host has dimension equal to the number of Θ-classes.

The key insight is that the geodesic we constructed for the hypercube — descend to the
meet, ascend to the join — is available precisely when local geodesic data glue into a
global tree, which is a purely combinatorial closure condition. Why now? Our
`hypercube_isometric` result exhibits the meet-join geodesic in the cleanest possible
setting; abstracting the gluing step is the natural route to a host-recognition criterion
that does not presuppose an embedding.

open Matrix SimpleGraph
open scoped BigOperators

namespace SpectralFF

variable {n : ℕ} (G : SimpleGraph (Fin n)) [DecidableRel G.Adj]

/-! ## The Rayleigh quotient and spectral radius -/

/-- The Rayleigh quotient of the adjacency operator at a vector `x`:
`(xᵀ A x) / (xᵀ x)`. -/
noncomputable def rquo (x : Fin n → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (x ⬝ᵥ (G.adjMatrix ℝ *ᵥ x)) / (x ⬝ᵥ x)

/-- The **spectral radius** of `G`: the supremum of the Rayleigh quotient of the
adjacency operator over all nonzero vectors. -/
noncomputable def specRad : ℝ :=
  ⨆ x : {x : Fin n → ℝ // x ≠ 0}, rquo G x.1

The numerator of the Rayleigh quotient expands over the neighbourhoods.
-/
lemma quadForm_eq (x : Fin n → ℝ) :
    x ⬝ᵥ (G.adjMatrix ℝ *ᵥ x) = ∑ i, ∑ j ∈ G.neighborFinset i, x i * x j := by
  simp +decide [ SimpleGraph.neighborFinset_eq_filter, Matrix.mulVec, dotProduct ];
  simp +decide [ Finset.sum_ite, Finset.mul_sum _ _ _ ]

Double counting over the symmetric adjacency relation:
`∑_i ∑_{j ∼ i} g j = ∑_j d(j) · g j`.
-/
lemma sum_neighbor_swap (g : Fin n → ℝ) :

  simp +decide only [neighborFinset_eq_filter, Finset.sum_filter];
  rw [ Finset.sum_comm ];
  simp +decide [ SimpleGraph.degree, SimpleGraph.neighborFinset_def ];
  simp +decide [ Finset.sum_ite, SimpleGraph.adj_comm ]
